client: Luna, I've been feeling really overwhelmed by my new job at the marketing agency. It seems like everyone else on my team has so much more experience, and I constantly worry that I'm falling behind or not meeting expectations. I sometimes wonder if therapy can actually help me with this pressure and anxiety.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling quite a bit of pressure with your new job, and it's understandable to worry about meeting expectations, especially when comparing yourself to others. Your feelings of being overwhelmed are valid, and it's good that you're considering how therapy can support you through this. What do you think might help you manage these feelings of anxiety and pressure in your work environment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you acknowledging how I feel, but honestly, I’m not sure what might help. I’ve tried deep breathing and some time management techniques, but they just feel temporary. It’s hard to shake off the nagging thought that I’m not good enough compared to my colleagues, and I worry that any strategies I try might not actually make a difference.
therapist: It seems like you're feeling quite stuck and uncertain about what might help, which can be really frustrating. It’s normal to feel that way, especially when you're trying strategies that don’t seem to stick. Can you share more about the thoughts that come up when you compare yourself to your colleagues? It might be helpful to explore those feelings together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I compare myself to my colleagues, I often think that they must have it all figured out while I’m just faking it. It makes me feel like an imposter, like I don’t deserve to be there. I know everyone has their struggles, but it’s hard to remember that when I’m feeling so anxious and out of place. I wonder if just talking about these comparisons will really help me feel any better.
therapist: It’s clear that the feelings of being an imposter and questioning your place at work are weighing heavily on you, and it’s understandable to feel anxious when you’re comparing yourself to others. While it might feel daunting to talk about these comparisons, sometimes just voicing those thoughts can help lighten the load and provide a new perspective. What do you think would change for you if you were able to challenge those feelings of not deserving to be there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: If I could challenge those feelings, I think it would help me feel more confident and less anxious about my work. I might be able to focus on what I can bring to the team instead of fixating on my perceived shortcomings. But honestly, it feels really difficult to let go of those thoughts, especially since they’ve been so ingrained in how I view myself for so long. I’m not sure how to start changing that.
therapist: It sounds like you have a strong desire to shift your focus from those negative comparisons to recognizing what you truly bring to the team, which is a powerful insight. I can sense the struggle you're experiencing with those ingrained thoughts, and it’s completely okay to feel that way. What small steps do you think you could take to begin challenging those beliefs about yourself? Sometimes even tiny shifts can lead to a bigger change over time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess one small step could be to keep a journal where I write down my accomplishments, even the little ones, to remind myself of what I do well. But I worry that I might forget to do it or that it won’t really change how I feel about myself. It just seems hard to believe that writing things down would make a real difference when those negative thoughts feel so powerful.
therapist: It's great that you've identified keeping a journal as a small step to recognize your accomplishments, even the little ones. It’s completely natural to feel skeptical about whether this practice can make a difference, especially when those negative thoughts feel so strong. What do you think might help you stay committed to this journaling practice, and how can we make it feel more manageable for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think setting a specific time each day to write in the journal could help me stay committed. But I also worry that I might forget or feel too overwhelmed to do it on tough days. It feels like I’m already juggling so much, and adding one more thing might just make it feel like another task I have to check off, rather than something that actually helps.
therapist: I can see that you're feeling quite overwhelmed by the idea of adding journaling to your routine, and it’s understandable to be concerned about it feeling like just another task. It’s important that whatever you choose to do feels supportive rather than burdensome. What if we brainstormed some ways to make journaling feel lighter or more enjoyable on those tough days?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of making journaling feel lighter, but I’m not sure what that would look like in practice. Maybe I could try writing just a few sentences instead of a whole page? But even then, I still worry that on tough days, I might just avoid it altogether because it feels like one more thing to think about. It’s hard to envision a way to make it feel easy and not like a chore.
therapist: It sounds like you're really trying to find a way to make journaling feel more accessible for you, which is a positive step. Writing just a few sentences is a great idea, and it might help to think of it more as a moment of reflection rather than a task. What if you allowed yourself to be flexible with it—maybe on tougher days, you could just jot down one positive thought or even a single word that represents how you feel? How does that approach resonate with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think the idea of jotting down just one word or a positive thought feels a bit more manageable, and it takes the pressure off. But I still worry that even on tough days, I might end up not doing it at all because it can feel overwhelming to even think about. I guess I’m just unsure if that little shift would really help me break through those feelings of anxiety and self-doubt.
therapist: It’s wonderful to hear that the idea of jotting down a single word or positive thought feels more manageable for you. It’s completely natural to have concerns about whether these small shifts can really help with anxiety and self-doubt, especially when those feelings are so strong. What do you think could support you on those tough days to gently remind you to take that small step, even if it feels overwhelming?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think maybe setting a reminder on my phone could help me remember to take that small step, but I also worry that I might just ignore it when it goes off. It feels like I’m battling against my own mind sometimes, so even having a reminder might not be enough to push me to do it. I want to believe that these little changes can help, but I’m just not sure how to make them stick when I’m feeling so anxious.
therapist: It's great that you're considering setting a reminder on your phone, as that could be a helpful nudge. I hear your concern about potentially ignoring it, and it’s understandable to feel like you're battling against your own mind at times. What if we explored some ways to make that reminder feel more inviting or encouraging, so it becomes a gentle prompt rather than a pressure? What might help you feel more connected to that small step on days when anxiety feels stronger?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate that you're trying to help me find a way to make the reminders feel more inviting.
